A merge records a new commit with two parents, so the history shows that two lines of work existed and were joined. The firm rule is never to rebase commits that other people have already pulled, because rebasing rewrites them with new identifiers and everyone else's copy suddenly disagrees with yours. 40.before: A B-tree keeps keys sorted in wide, shallow nodes. Each node holds many keys and pointers to children, so a lookup starts at the root, compares the key with the few values in that node, and follows exactly one pointer down. Because every node is wide, even a table with millions of rows is usually only three or four levels deep, which means three or four page reads instead of scanning every row. Range queries are cheap too: once the first matching key is found, the leaves are linked, so the database walks along them in order. The cost is on writes. Every insert or update to an indexed column must also update the tree, and occasionally split a full node. That is why indexing every column is a bad idea: reads on the indexed columns get faster while every write gets slower, and the indexes take disk space. A good rule is to index the columns that appear in frequent WHERE clauses and joins, check the query plan to confirm the index is used, and drop indexes nothing reads.

53.before: Normalisation organises tables so each fact is stored once, which stops updates from leaving copies that disagree. First normal form asks that every column hold a single value: no lists of phone numbers squeezed into one field, and no repeating groups of columns such as phone1, phone2 and phone3. Second normal form applies to tables with a composite key and asks that every other column depend on the whole key, not on part of it; a course name stored in an enrolment table keyed by student and course depends only on the course, so it belongs in a course table. Third normal form asks that columns depend on the key and nothing else, so a city stored next to a postcode, where the city follows from the postcode, moves into its own table. The practical test is to ask where you would have to change something if a fact changed. If the answer is several rows, the design invites inconsistency. Reporting databases sometimes denormalise on purpose to make reads faster.

It runs in milliseconds and points straight at the line that broke. An integration test checks that several real parts work together: the code talking to an actual database, two services calling each other, or a request going through the whole web stack. A healthy suite has many unit tests for logic, a smaller number of integration tests for the seams where components meet, and a handful of end-to-end tests for the most important user journeys. Cache-Control tells a browser or proxy how long it may reuse a response without asking the server again: max-age is the number of seconds, no-store forbids keeping it at all, and private means only the user's own browser may keep it, not a shared proxy. An ETag is a label for one version of a resource, often a hash of its content. When the cached copy expires, the browser sends the label back in an If-None-Match header. If the content has not changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, which saves bandwidth even though a round trip still happens. Used together they give fast pages without stale data: long max-age for files whose names change when their content changes, such as bundled scripts with a hash in the file name, and short max-age plus an ETag for pages that change in place. The most common mistake is caching a personalised page in a shared proxy, which is exactly what private exists to prevent.

83.before: TCP gives you a reliable, ordered stream. It sets up a connection with a handshake, numbers every byte, resends anything that is lost, and slows down when the network is congested. The price is latency: a lost packet holds up everything behind it until it is resent. UDP sends independent datagrams with no connection, no ordering and no retransmission; a packet either arrives or it does not, and the application decides what to do about it. TCP suits anything where every byte matters and a short delay is acceptable, such as web pages, file transfers and database connections. UDP suits real-time traffic where a late packet is worse than a missing one: voice and video calls, online games, and DNS lookups that are small enough to simply retry. Modern protocols blur the line. QUIC, which carries HTTP/3, runs over UDP but builds its own reliability and encryption on top, so that one lost packet only delays the stream it belongs to rather than every stream on the connection.

90.before: Most languages store decimals as binary floating point numbers, and many simple decimal fractions have no exact binary representation, in the same way that one third has no exact decimal one. The values stored for 0.1 and 0.2 are therefore very slightly off, and their sum lands on a binary value that prints as 0.30000000000000004. The error is tiny but it matters in two places. Comparisons should not test floats for exact equality; check that the difference is smaller than a small tolerance instead. And money should not be stored as floats at all, because rounding errors add up across many transactions and auditors expect exact cents. The usual choices for money are integers counting the smallest unit, such as cents, or a decimal type that stores numbers in base ten. Very large and very small values also lose precision in floating point, so summing many numbers of different sizes is more accurate if the small ones are added first.

109.before: For an array, reading by index is constant time, while searching for a value is linear because in the worst case every element is checked. Appending to a dynamic array is constant on average, though an occasional resize copies everything. Inserting at the front of an array is linear, since every element shifts. A linked list flips some of these: inserting at a known node is constant, but finding that node is linear. A hash table gives constant average time for insert, lookup and delete, with a linear worst case when many keys collide. A balanced binary search tree gives logarithmic time for all three and keeps keys in order, which a hash table does not. A binary heap gives constant time to peek at the smallest element and logarithmic time to insert or remove it, which is why priority queues use one. Sorting by comparison costs n log n at best. These numbers describe growth, not speed: a linear scan over a small array often beats a hash lookup in practice because of memory locality.
